title: 🐉 Creatures & the Natural World
rawNotionMarkup: Eryndor has a full natural world: ordinary animals, livestock, working animals, pests, predators, fish, birds and insects, alongside magical creatures, ancient beings and dangerous legendary life. Wildlife exists for ecological reasons; it does not exist solely to challenge Gloin. ## Principles of the living world - Establish ordinary fauna and believable ecosystems alongside extraordinary creatures. - Species have habitats, ranges, diets, breeding cycles, migration patterns, territories and seasonal behaviour. - Mountain ranges, forests, plains, wetlands, deserts, coasts, rivers, cultivated land and underground systems should support different ecologies. - Magical creatures are part of the natural world where appropriate, but magic does not make every animal supernatural. - Hunting, herding, fishing, trapping, animal husbandry, conservation, pest control and wildlife trade are ordinary parts of economies and cultures. - Creatures can be dangerous without being evil. Many avoid unnecessary conflict; others are territorial, hungry, defensive, diseased, habituated to people or genuinely predatory. - Keep known species, local reports, folklore, mistaken identification and unverified sightings distinct. - A creature's behaviour should make ecological and practical sense. Do not make every encounter an attack. - Ordinary animals coexist alongside intelligent animal peoples. Those peoples are persons with societies, not just unusually clever wildlife. ## Broad categories of life ### Ordinary wildlife and livestock The world includes familiar domestic and wild animals, working animals, pests, predators, fish, birds and insects. Their presence should reflect regional habitat, climate, agriculture and trade. Livestock and working animals support food production, transport, herding, craft, military logistics and household life. Their cost, care, feed, health and seasonal needs should matter where relevant. ### Intelligent peoples with animal traits Wolvenkin, Foxfolk, Lionfolk, Tigerfolk, Elephantfolk, Bearfolk, Cowfolk and Pigfolk are established sentient animal peoples. They have families, societies, traditions and political interests. Animal traits may influence senses, instincts, movement and physical behaviour, but they are not ordinary animals wearing clothes. Other intelligent peoples are recorded on Peoples & Cultures. Do not add new species to the setting without the user's explicit approval. ### Magical creatures Magical creatures exist, but not every strange animal is magical and not every magical creature is a monster. Their abilities, habitats, life cycles, limits and relationship to Natural Magic or lunar influences should be established individually. Do not assume every magical creature derives its nature from a particular moon. Lunar influence can affect creatures and ecosystems, but the exact relationship depends on the species and circumstances. ### Ancient and legendary beings Some intelligent or extraordinary beings occupy a place between ecology, history and legend. Their classification should respect their actual nature rather than treating every large being as a monster. #### Drakari — true dragons Drakari are rare, intelligent true dragons numbering fewer than 10,000 across Eryndor. They have ancient courts and territories. They are not interchangeable beasts, and their personalities range from noble and philosophical to vain, possessive or cruel. Their intelligence, power and long histories make them political and individual actors as much as creatures. The details of dragon biology, age ranges, flight, reproduction, magical abilities, court structures and regional populations remain to be established rather than invented as a complete universal taxonomy. #### Ents Ents are ancient, patient, contemplative beings deeply connected to the natural world. They are protective of forests and living things and tend to think in seasons, generations and centuries. They are distinct from ordinary trees and from Living Mountains. #### Giants Giants are powerful, independent beings who may live alone or in close-knit mountain and highland communities. Their physical scale does not make them simple-minded. They are a people with varied temperaments, not a generic monster class. #### Living Mountains Living Mountains are genuine, exceedingly rare colossal living beings. When dormant, their bodies can be indistinguishable from natural mountain ranges or solitary peaks. They may remain dormant for centuries or millennia while forests, rivers, caves, snow and even settlements accumulate across them. Awakening is extraordinarily rare. It is not caused by ordinary noise, mining or routine lunar alignment. The conditions are not fully understood and may differ between individuals. If one awakens, terrain may shift, valleys may close, rivers may change course and settlements built upon its body may be endangered. Living Mountains are not automatically hostile or benevolent. Their motives, awareness and relationships with smaller peoples vary and may be difficult to comprehend. Their number, locations, origins and individual natures remain unknown. They are distinct from Giants and Ents, not ordinary monsters or convenient mounts and weapons. ## Ecological regions and environment Eryndor's geography produces varied habitats. Wildlife and magical ecology should be developed in context as locations become relevant: - Ironspine Mountains: High-altitude, rocky and subterranean habitats; mountain fauna, caves, underground water and mining environments. - Letharion and other forests: Woodland ecosystems with seasonal cycles, canopy, undergrowth, rivers and old-growth habitats. - Eastern Grasslands and plains: Open-country grazers, herd animals, predators, burrowing species and migratory life. - Wetlands, rivers and estuaries: Fish, amphibious life, water birds, marsh plants and species adapted to changing water levels. - Sahrad's deserts and river valleys: Heat, drought, oasis and river ecosystems, with sharply different life in dry and fertile zones. - Tharvorn's tundra and frozen regions: Cold-adapted wildlife, seasonal migration, snow and ice environments. - Orundel's jungles and great rivers: Dense and diverse habitats with specialised canopy, river and wetland species. - Vaelora's forests, coasts and lakes: Woodland, rugged shoreline, freshwater and mountainous ecosystems. These are broad habitat expectations, not a complete catalogue of established animals. Do not invent a detailed regional bestiary without recording new species deliberately. ## Behaviour, danger and encounter design - Animals generally seek food, shelter, mates, safety and territory rather than combat. - Predators may stalk, test, threaten or retreat according to hunger, risk and opportunity. - Herbivores can be dangerous when cornered, protecting young or defending territory. - Intelligent creatures and peoples have reasons, values and relationships beyond their combat abilities. - Injuries, disease, hunger, weather, habitat loss, migration and human activity affect wildlife. - Hunting or killing a creature can have ecological, social, economic or legal consequences. - Not every encounter needs to be resolved through violence. Observation, avoidance, negotiation, tracking, rescue and coexistence are possible. ## Bestiary entries and evidence standards When a specific creature is established, record: - Name and alternate regional names. - Classification: ordinary animal, magical creature, intelligent people, ancient being or uncertain. - Habitat and geographic range. - Physical description, size and distinguishing features. - Diet, behaviour, social structure and life cycle. - Abilities, limitations and vulnerabilities. - Relationship with people, livestock, trade and the local environment. - Cultural beliefs, folklore and verified observations. - Evidence status: established, reported, disputed, hypothesis or unknown. Do not convert a local rumour into a global species fact. Similar-looking creatures may be unrelated, and names may refer to different animals in different regions. ## Ecological canon boundaries - The existence of dragons, Ents, Giants and Living Mountains does not mean every mountain, forest or cave contains a legendary being. - Living Mountains are a rare form of colossal sentient life, distinct from Giants and Ents. Their locations and number remain unknown. - New intelligent peoples belong in Peoples & Cultures as well as this page when their biology and ecology materially matter. - The existence of the nine additional peoples listed here is established. Their detailed biology, cultures, reputations, behaviours and ecological roles remain subject to development and revision. - Ordinary wildlife should be developed with the same care as magical beasts. Eryndor is not populated only by monsters. - Do not tie every unusual creature, ecosystem or ancient being to the First Throne, lunar cataclysms or the eastern mine mystery. ## Small settlements within the natural world Eryndor's inhabited landscape is not limited to major cities, fortresses and great civilisations. Small villages, hamlets, family steadings, burrow communities, woodland enclaves and modest hidden settlements belonging to lesser magical peoples may be found throughout suitable environments. Potential habitats include forest clearings and ancient woodland, open plains and grassland edges, hills and river valleys, marshes, mountain foothills, natural cave systems and worked underground networks, as well as coastal inlets, islands, reefs and underwater regions where the inhabitants can live. Ocean communities may be on the shore, among islands, beneath the surface or in submerged habitats; their exact form must suit the people and environment. These communities should feel ecologically and economically grounded. Consider water, food, shelter, building materials, climate, predators, magical hazards, access routes, trade, seasonal movement and relations with nearby settlements. Some are known to travellers; others are hidden, isolated, nomadic or only reached with a guide. Some trade with larger peoples, while others prefer limited contact. Not every settlement is friendly, hostile, wealthy, poor or in need of rescue. This establishes the desired presence and distribution of small communities, including communities belonging to the nine additional peoples now established in Eryndor. It does not establish a fixed list of named settlements or precise locations. Create individual settlements with a distinct habitat, scale, local character and plausible ecological support; do not invent a dense network of named places or claim precise locations before the geography is developed. ## Additional peoples — established ecological canon The nine peoples listed below are established intelligent peoples of Eryndor, not automatically monsters or wildlife. The ecological and biological concepts in this section are current canon, subject to future revision by the creator. Where a trait, mechanism, range or life-history detail is explicitly described as unknown, uncertain or requiring further development, it remains unresolved rather than being silently filled in. ### Kobolds Potential habitats include caverns, cliff systems, old quarries, ravines and engineered burrows. Small body size may favour narrow passages and compact dwellings, but communities still require ventilation, clean water, food sources, waste management and safe exits. Tunnel engineering can create hazards for neighbouring ecosystems through drainage changes, spoil heaps, smoke or unstable excavation. Their exact temperature tolerance, diet and reproduction remain open. ### Satyrs / Fauns Potential habitats include woodland edges, hills, meadows, orchards and broken uplands. Caprine locomotion may suit steep or uneven terrain but create limitations on smooth, icy or waterlogged ground. Plant-rich diets require seasonal food planning, access to browse and pasture, and careful management of woodland regeneration. The distinction between Satyrs and Fauns remains unresolved. ### Pixies Potential habitats include forest canopies, meadow margins, reed beds, cliffs and small sheltered spaces within larger settlements. Powered flight would be constrained by wind, rain, cold, fatigue, wing injury, body mass and carried weight. Their small size implies high relative energy needs, rapid heat loss and vulnerability to ordinary predators and weather. Tiny settlements still require agriculture, gathering or reliable trade at an appropriate scale. ### Minotaurs Potential habitats include grasslands, foothills, broad valleys and settled agricultural regions, though no single range is established. Large bodies require substantial food, water, cooling and durable shelter. Horns and body proportions affect movement through dense forest, narrow tunnels and ordinary doorways. Their grazing or mixed diet, herd relationships and environmental impact need deliberate development rather than assumption. ### Brownies / Boggarts Potential habitats include farmsteads, barns, mills, hedgerows, root-cellars, village margins and abandoned buildings. Small terrestrial bodies may make use of existing human-scale structures, but require independent food, water, shelter and family life. Any quiet movement or low-light adaptation should have biological limits. Brownie and Boggart may be related lineages, separate peoples or outsider labels; this is not decided. ### Ogres Potential habitats include forest margins, mountain valleys, river corridors and agricultural settlements. Large body mass means high caloric and water demands, pressure on local food supplies, difficulty using small infrastructure and a need for appropriately sized tools and shelter. Their impact on forests, grazing and fisheries should be considered alongside their economic contributions. ### Trolls Potential habitats may include cold uplands, damp valleys, rocky river systems, caves and wetlands, depending on lineage. Thick skin, slow metabolism and torpor are not universal troll traits; whether particular lineages possess any of these adaptations remains unresolved. If regeneration is developed, it must have limits and resource costs. Troll communities affect rivers, bridges, caves and local wildlife like any other settled people; folklore about sunlight or invulnerability is not confirmed biology. ### Mushroom folk Potential habitats include damp forests, old-growth root systems, wetlands, caves and underground chambers with suitable substrates. Their fungal biology may depend on moisture, temperature, mineral availability, organic matter and symbiotic relationships. Spore dispersal, reproduction and any shared mycelial communication need careful limits; spores must not be treated as automatic infection or mind control. Individual identity and agency remain central. ### Harpies Potential habitats include cliffs, highlands, sea stacks and open coastal terrain with suitable take-off and landing areas. Powered flight imposes strict limits on body mass, wing area, weather tolerance and cargo. Flightless, injured or elderly individuals need viable mobility and social inclusion. Fishing, hunting, gathering or trade may support some communities, but no single diet or occupation is assumed. ### Ecological and classification safeguards - The existence of these nine peoples in Eryndor is established canon: Kobolds, Satyrs/Fauns, Pixies, Minotaurs, Brownies/Boggarts, Ogres, Trolls, Mushroom folk and Harpies. Their current ecological concepts and descriptions are accepted canon and may be revised by the creator at any time. Specific details explicitly marked unknown or unresolved remain open; do not invent answers merely because the people themselves are now established. - Treat them as intelligent peoples with social, economic and environmental relationships, not as encounter-table monsters. - Build food webs, resource needs, waste, disease, reproduction, migration and settlement impacts consistently. - Magical abilities, if any, must be defined separately from ordinary biology and should not be assumed to derive from a particular moon. - No precise population, lifespan, range, settlement or continent assignment is established. - Preserve ecological diversity: not every forest, plain, cave or ocean contains every established people. Their actual ranges and settlement locations should be grounded in suitable habitats and established geography. - Their presence should not erase established peoples or imply kinship with them without approval. ## Encounter design — preserve familiar fantasy danger The established reputations, behaviour and rarity of unusually kind individuals for the nine additional peoples are recorded in [Peoples & Cultures](https://app.notion.com/p/41ea4939d3718163955ced679e3f56bf). That page is the single reference for the current reputation spectrum; this page applies it to ecology, creature behaviour and encounter design rather than duplicating the same list. These concepts are canon and may be revised by the creator. Eryndor should retain familiar fantasy folklore and genuine danger. The big bad wolf in the dark woods, harpies threatening travellers from above, a Minotaur rampaging through a settlement and an ogre raiding a farmstead all belong in the world where the habitat, history and circumstances support them. - Some dangerous encounters involve intelligent peoples; others involve ordinary predators, magical beasts or other non-sapient creatures. Keep those categories distinct. - Not every threat needs to be morally complex. A predator may simply hunt; a malicious individual or raiding band may knowingly terrorise others. - Do not make every member of a feared people evil. Rare decent individuals remain possible, and for some peoples exceptionally unusual. - Reputation has practical consequences: villagers may bar gates, warn travellers, organise watches, protect livestock, avoid certain routes or pass down frightening stories. - A frightening reputation should have a plausible basis in local history, repeated encounters, observed behaviour or cultural memory. It may also be exaggerated, misunderstood or contradicted by another region. - Encounter danger should reflect numbers, terrain, hunger, territory, season, intelligence, motivation, preparation and available escape routes. Do not use species identity alone as a complete encounter script. - A creature or people should not appear in every habitat by default. Use the ecological range and settlement context recorded for that people, and preserve regional variation. Guiding balance: Familiar fantasy at its heart. Ecological and individual depth should enrich danger and wonder, not erase them.
